1.title: The Decision to Deploy: Context, Models and Options
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: The Decision to Deploy. Domain four moves to the deployer's side. Before an organization puts an A I system to work, it should understand the setting, choose a type of model, and choose where and how to run it. This module covers all three, and the risks each choice brings.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Check the setting of a use case: goals, performance needs, data, ethics and people. Tell apart model types: predictive or generative, closed or open, small or large, text-only or multimodal. Tell apart deployment options: cloud, on-premises or edge, and as is, fine-tuned, retrieval-augmented or agentic. Spot the risks each choice brings. And reach a decision: go, go with conditions, or no-go.

1.title: Case Check-In: Choosing the Assistant's Model and Setup
1.text: At Helios, Anika Berg, the Customer Support director, wants the customer assistant to answer service questions faster. The goal is clear, but some support documents are out of date, and the support staff need training. The team weighs a large closed model from Corvid Labs against a small open model it could host itself. It also weighs retrieved documents against fine-tuning, and holds back an agentic meeting-booking function. Samira Haddad asks: go, go with conditions, or no-go?

1.title: Start With the Use Case: Five Context Factors
1.text: Before any model is chosen, define the setting. There are five factors. Goals: the problem, the benefit expected and how success will be measured. Performance needs: how accurate, fast, available and explainable the system must be. Data: what exists, how good it is and whether it may be used. Ethics and risk: who could be affected and how much oversight is needed. And people and skills: who will operate, check and rely on it. Exam tip: the context comes first and the model second. A model chosen before the use case is understood is a guess.

1.title: Goals and Performance Needs: What Good Enough Means
1.text: A clear goal names the problem, the user and the measure of success. Performance requirements turn the goal into numbers: accuracy, error tolerance, speed, availability, explainability and cost. Tolerance for error follows harm. A wrong film suggestion is cheap; a wrong hiring ranking is not. Set thresholds before testing, as module nine said, and review them if the use changes. A need that cannot be measured cannot be shown to be met. At Helios, the assistant must answer in seconds, in plain language, and say when it does not know. Exam tip: the cost of a wrong output sets the bar.

1.title: Data Availability: Can the Use Case Be Fed?
1.text: Every use case runs on data. Ask four questions. Do the data exist? Are they good enough: accurate, complete and current? May we use them: is there a lawful basis, a clear purpose and a license? And do they represent real use? Missing or poor data may rule a use case out, or change the approach: collect first, narrow the scope, or use a pre-trained model. At Helios, the support documents exist, but some are old, so fixing them comes before go-live. Exam tip: no suitable data, no suitable use case. Say so before money is spent on a model.

1.title: Ethics and Risk Appetite: Who Is Affected?
1.text: Ask who is affected, how seriously, and whether the effect can be undone. Work, credit, health and education set high bars in law and ethics, as modules one, five and six showed. Ask about human oversight: does a person review the output, or does the system act alone? Risk appetite is the level of risk the organization accepts, set by leaders and the committee. The matrix shows the pattern. The more a system affects people, and the more it acts on its own, the stronger the controls, up to a decision not to deploy. Exam tip: weigh effect and autonomy together.

1.title: Workforce Readiness and the Go or No-Go Decision
1.text: People and skills: can staff use the tool, check its output and escalate problems? Module two covered training. Change management: roles shift, so plan communication, support and a feedback route. Capacity: who will monitor and maintain the system after launch? The decision has three outcomes: go, go with conditions, such as training first, or no-go. The context findings feed the model and option choices, and then the impact assessment in module twelve. At Helios, support agents learn when to correct the assistant before launch. Exam tip: a sound system still fails if the people around it are not ready.

1.title: Classic and Generative Models
1.text: Classic, or predictive, models score, classify or predict, often from structured data: a ranking, a yes or no, a number. Generative models create new content: text, images, code or audio. Classic models have a narrow task and outputs that are easier to measure. Generative models take on broad tasks, with open-ended outputs that are harder to test. Classic risks include biased scores, opacity and poor data. Generative models add confabulation, harmful content, leakage and intellectual property questions. At Helios, the hiring tool is predictive and the assistant is generative. Exam tip: open-ended output means open-ended failure modes.

1.title: What Generative AI Adds to the Risk List
1.text: The N I S T generative A I profile names twelve risks that are unique to, or made worse by, generative A I, as module one said. Content: confabulation, dangerous, violent or hateful content, obscene or abusive content, and information integrity. Data and rights: data privacy and intellectual property. Security: information security, and chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear information or capabilities. People and systems: human-A I configuration, and harmful bias or homogenization. Supply chain and planet: value chain and component integration, and environmental impacts. Choosing a generative model means deciding which apply. Exam tip: expect confabulation, privacy leaks and intellectual property.

1.title: Proprietary and Open-Source Models
1.text: Proprietary, or closed, models are owned by a provider and reached through an interface. Their internals and training data are usually not visible. Open-source or open-weight models make the weights public, so you can inspect, host and adapt them. Closed models bring provider-managed updates and support, with less control. Open models bring control and transparency, but more work for you in hosting, security, testing and updates. Licenses differ, and open models can carry usage limits, so read them. Either way, the deployer must evaluate the model for its own use. At Helios, the Corvid Labs model is closed. Exam tip: open does not mean risk-free.

1.title: Open Source and the Law
1.text: The A I Act gives open source a partial exemption. Under Article two, point twelve, systems released under free and open-source licenses are largely outside the Act, unless they are high-risk, prohibited under Article five, or subject to transparency duties under Article fifty. For general-purpose models, Article fifty-three, point two, exempts open-source providers from the technical documentation and downstream information duties. They still owe the copyright policy and the training-content summary, and the exemption is lost for systemic-risk models. G D P R, product liability and other laws apply whatever the license. Exam tip: the exemption is partial.

1.title: Small and Large Models
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Large models offer broad abilities and varied tasks, but at higher cost per use, with slower responses, and they are harder to test fully. Small models are narrower, cheaper and faster, and can run on your own hardware or a device. They may need retrieval or fine-tuning to reach the quality you need. The rule is fit over size: choose the smallest model that meets the requirements. Small models can keep data in-house. Test both on your own tasks, because public benchmarks may not reflect your use. Exam tip: bigger is not automatically better or safer.

1.title: Language and Multimodal Models
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Language models work with text, including code. Multimodal models take in or produce images, audio and video as well as text. They open new uses: reading scans and charts, describing images, voice assistants and video analysis. They also bring new risks: deepfakes and synthetic media, covered by the Article fifty transparency duties; biometric and sensitive data in faces and voices; hidden instructions in images; and more ways to attack the system. Test each input type, and check the data rights for each. At Helios, the hiring tool's video interview raises these questions. Exam tip: every added modality adds questions.

1.title: Matching the Model Type to the Task
1.text: Start from the task, not from the technology. To rank, classify or predict, use classic models. To draft, summarize or answer, use generative language models. For images, audio and video, use multimodal models. Then decide between closed or open, and small or large, based on control needs, cost, data sensitivity and testing. The table pairs four tasks with a model type and the main risk to weigh. Record the reasons in the decision record, so that the choice can be reviewed later. Exam tip: match the model type to the task and the risk, and write down why.

2.title: Where It Runs: Cloud, On-Premises or Edge
2.text: Three places to run a model. Cloud means a provider's infrastructure: quick to start, scalable and lighter to maintain. On-premises means your own data centers: the most control over data and security, but you buy and run everything. Edge means on the device, such as a phone, a camera or a vehicle: fast, works offline and keeps data local, but with limited power and harder updates. Hybrid setups mix these. The drivers are data sensitivity, speed, cost, skills and laws on data location. Exam tip: where the system runs decides who controls the data, the security and the updates.

2.title: Cloud Deployment: Shared Responsibility and Data Location
2.text: In the cloud, responsibility is shared. The provider secures the infrastructure; the customer secures its data, its access settings and its use. Data location matters: moving personal data across borders must meet the G D P R transfer rules in Articles forty-four to forty-nine, so check where the provider processes and stores data. Contract terms matter too: use of your data for the provider's own training, logging and retention, sub-processors, audit rights and incident notice. Watch for lock-in and concentration risk. At Helios, the assistant reaches its model through a cloud interface. Exam tip: the cloud does not move legal responsibility for the data.

2.title: On-Premises and Edge: Control, Cost and Maintenance
2.text: On-premises deployment keeps data inside your boundary. You set security and access, and strict data rules are easier to meet. The price is cost and effort: hardware, specialists, patching, capacity planning and your own monitoring. Edge deployment reduces transfers and delay, which helps where the network is poor or the data are sensitive. But edge brings small models, limited power, many devices to update and secure, and physical access risks. A flaw in a model on thousands of devices needs a patch and withdrawal plan. At Helios, hosting an open model would add duties the team lacks today. Exam tip: more control means more work.

2.title: How the Model Is Used: A Ladder of Adaptation
2.text: Now, how the model is used. Look at the ladder. As is: the model with careful prompts and guardrails, which takes the least effort and gives the least fit. Retrieval-augmented: the model answers using documents fetched at the moment of the question. Fine-tuned: the model is trained further on your data to change its behavior. Agentic: the model plans steps and uses tools to act. Combinations are common. Start with the least adaptation that meets the need, because each step up adds effort, cost and risk to govern. Exam tip: try the simplest approach first.

2.title: Using the Model As Is: Prompts, Guardrails and Other Techniques
2.text: Using a model as is does not mean using it carelessly. Prompt design, with instructions, examples and a system prompt, shapes behavior without changing the model. Guardrails add input and output filters, topic limits, blocked actions and fallbacks to a person. Other techniques include parameter settings, caching, combining models, and distillation, where a small model is trained to imitate a larger one. The limits: the model's knowledge and flaws stay the same, and clever inputs can bypass guardrails. Record the prompt and settings as part of the system version, and test them. Exam tip: prompts and settings are part of the system.

2.title: Fine-Tuning: Benefits, Risks and Role Changes
2.text: Fine-tuning means further training on your own examples to change style, format or domain behavior. The benefits are better fit, shorter prompts and sometimes a smaller model. The risks are leakage of training data in outputs, bias in the new data, drift from the original safety behavior, extra cost, and the need to retest everything. The fine-tuning data need the same lineage, quality and rights checks as any training data, as module nine said. And roles can change: a substantial modification of a high-risk system can make the deployer its provider, under Article twenty-five. Exam tip: fine-tune for behavior and style; use retrieval for facts that change.

2.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Grounding on Your Documents
2.text: With retrieval, the system searches your documents for relevant passages, adds them to the prompt, and the model answers from them, ideally with a source. The benefits: answers use current company content, you can update documents without retraining, and sources can be shown. But retrieval reduces confabulation; it does not remove it. The risks are stale or wrong documents, as in the Helios refund error, weak access control, injection through documents, and poor retrieval. Give the knowledge source owners, review dates and versions, and test both retrieval and answers. Exam tip: the document source is part of the system.

2.title: Agentic Architectures: Autonomy and Excessive Agency
2.text: Agentic systems plan multi-step tasks and use tools, such as calendars, email, payments or code, to act on their own. The new risk is that a mistake or a manipulated instruction becomes a real action, quickly and at scale. The O W A S P list calls the problem excessive agency: more functions, permissions or autonomy than the task needs. The controls are least-privilege tools, limits on actions and spending, human approval for consequential steps, logging and a kill switch, as module ten said. At Helios, the meeting-booking function is held back until these are designed and tested. Exam tip: autonomy multiplies every other risk.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Context: goals, performance needs, data, ethics and risk, and people and skills, ending in go, go with conditions or no-go. Model types: classic or generative, closed or open, where the open-source exemptions are partial, small or large, where you choose the smallest that fits, and language or multimodal. Where it runs: cloud, on-premises or edge, and who controls data and updates. How it is used: as is, retrieval-augmented, fine-tuned or agentic, with the least adaptation that works. And the watch-outs for each.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Anika Berg wants the Helios assistant to answer service questions. The goal is clear and the support staff are trained, but the support documents are scattered, out of date and contradict one another. Which factor of the use-case context is the main concern? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The goal is clear and staff are trained, so the weak point is the data. Fix the documents before go-live.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A claims team plans to use A I to triage insurance claims. Which two questions belong in the context review before a model is chosen? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. The context review covers performance needs, including how much error is tolerable, and workforce readiness. Vendor branding, parameter counts and screen design are not context factors.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Which statement best describes a difference between proprietary and open-source models? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Open weights let the deployer inspect, host and adapt the model, and the deployer then owns more of the safety work. Closed models are not automatically safer, open models are not exempt from law, and only open weights can be downloaded and adapted.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. The Helios assistant mostly answers short, routine questions about services. A colleague proposes always using the largest available model. What is the best governance response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Fit matters more than size. A smaller model may meet the need at lower cost, with faster answers and easier testing, so test it, choose the smallest that works, and record the reasons.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A hospital needs an A I tool for dictated patient notes. Its policy says patient data must not leave the hospital network, and the tool must keep working during network outages. Which deployment option fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Keeping data inside the network and working offline point to on-premises or edge deployment. Cloud options send data out and depend on a connection.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which two statements about retrieval-augmented generation are correct? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. Retrieval grounds answers on documents, and lets the organization update knowledge by updating them. It does not change the weights, which is fine-tuning, it does not remove errors, and it needs no training from scratch.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Helios proposes an assistant function that books meetings for customers: it reads emails, checks calendars and sends invitations on its own. Which feature of this design calls for the most careful governance before deployment? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. An agentic function turns errors and manipulated instructions into actions, so it needs least-privilege permissions, limits, human approval, logging and a kill switch.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: C and E. Question three: A. Question four: D. Question five: B. Question six: A and E. Question seven: D. That completes Module eleven. Next, Module twelve: assessing the system, with impact assessments, vendor agreements and the risks of your own proprietary model.
